notes:
I found enough for notes on every verse. Most of it comes from older commentaries (Pulpit, Ellicott, Barnes, Gill, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Clarke, Keil & Delitzsch) and from David Guzik at enduringword.com. Two things are missing. I found nothing from Catholic, Orthodox, bibleodyssey.org or Lutheran sources, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so none of those appear below. I also couldn't open the gotquestions page on Romans 11:26 and only saw a summary of it in search results.

## vv. 1–8: The people's sin is the problem, not God

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: God's "hand" has lost none of its power. He isn't helping because of his people's sins, and he can't hear prayers that aren't sincere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: the people wondered whether God had grown weaker. He uses the verse to answer Harold Kushner's idea that God is loving but not all-powerful, which he says is not the God of the Bible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- Precept Austin collects a different application, that lack of faith "limits God." LACK OF FAITH LIMITS GOD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: "have separated" means a continuing action. Israel had been building the barrier for a long time, and its sins had made God turn his face away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: sin doesn't cut us off from God's presence or love. It does cut us off from fellowship with him, his blessing, some benefits of his love, and his protection. He also links the hidden face to Jesus' cry of forsakenness on the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- GotQuestions: because the people of Israel had violated the covenant God had made with them through Moses, the nation was separated from Him. https://www.gotquestions.org/put-words-in-your-mouth.html

**v. 3**
- Pulpit reads "blood" as child sacrifice to Moloch, persecution of prophets, and judicial murder, including corrupt justice that made people poor and shortened their lives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: the sense is that no one brings a lawsuit honestly. "Vanity" literally means chaos, a heap of false statements, so the whole basis of dealings between people was rotten. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik quotes Motyer: Isaiah is diagnosing, not just describing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: the viper's eggs are deadly plans, and the spider's web shows how flimsy they are. Anyone who joins in them dies spiritually, and crushing them only lets a viper out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik quotes Clarke: the webs are traps laid to catch poor neighbours. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary applies the webs to modern life, such as the web of a "respectable life" and of self-righteousness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-59.html

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the webs give no cover or protection. "Works of iniquity" is better rendered "works of nothingness," mere shams. Violence builds nothing; at best it destroys. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: their works will never cover them before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: people who can't build anything turn to destroying things. The language may point to a massacre of godly Israelites under Manasseh. Romans 3 quotes this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: peace comes only through righteousness, and crooked paths can only lead to destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: "peace" means shalom in its full sense. Paul uses vv. 7–8 in Romans 3:15–17 to show that humans are sinners "from head to toe." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/

## vv. 9–15a: The people confess

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: in vv. 9–15 Isaiah confesses on the people's behalf and counts himself among them. "Justice" here means God's judgment on Israel's enemies, which is held back because of Israel's sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: people who didn't care about justice and righteousness weren't given them. He compares Matthew 13:12. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: there was plenty of light, but they had no eyes to see it. The word translated "desolate places" appears only here and its meaning is uncertain; it may be "dark places." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: "roar" is better "growl." It pictures a low rumble of discontent alternating with despairing moans, like a dove's cooing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: their sins stand up as witnesses they can't refute, and serious sins haunt the memory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: the people have now had their "reality check" and stopped blaming God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/

**v. 13**
- Pulpit sorts the list into sins of the heart (treason against God, secret apostasy) and sins of the tongue (oppression, false accusation, lies). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit reads it as courtroom language: verdicts turned upside down, false witness beating true, and equity left waiting outside the court. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Howard Morrison: Isaiah's longest treatment of justice is in this chapter (vv. 4, 8, 11, 14, 15). https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_devotionals_1

## vv. 15b–21: God steps in himself

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: when truth fails, morality loses its foundation, and the honest person becomes prey for the ruthless. The verse division is misplaced: the first half belongs with the confession, the second half with God's response. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "wondered" describes God in human terms. Because no human champion appeared, God had to act in person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik: God would have preferred to work through a man or an intercessor, but his plan doesn't fail when none comes forward. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- Precept Austin's outline calls vv. 15b–21 the "Redeemer-Warrior." https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: the armour is clearly a metaphor, unlike the literal armour of Homer's gods. God carries no weapons, because the breath of his Spirit is enough. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm
- Guzik links this to Ephesians 6. It is "the armor of God" because it is his own, and he lets us use it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- Precept Austin agrees that it is from God and also his own armour. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_611
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary applies the "zeal" to Christ, for example as a boy in the Temple. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-59.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: "adversaries" are ungodly Israelites, and "enemies" are the heathen nations. "Islands" means the coastlands that joined in oppressing Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 19: translations differ**
- **KJV/NKJV:** "When the enemy comes in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD will lift up a standard." **Most modern versions:** "He will come like a rushing stream which the wind of the LORD drives."
- Cambridge Bible: the KJV follows the Targum, the Syriac and Jewish commentators. The RV reading is adopted by nearly all the best modern authorities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-19.htm
- Barnes: the KJV translators departed from all the ancient versions. It is true that God defends the church against attackers, yet this passage does not teach that doctrine, nor should it be so applied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-19.htm
- Ellicott: the KJV is at least as defensible as any other rendering. Pulpit keeps it too, reading the flood as the Euphrates (i.e. Assyria) and the Spirit as nearly a person. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/59-19.htm
- Calvin: the enemy's attack will look like it sweeps everything away, but God will make it subside at once. Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist on StudyLight): the rabbis applied this verse to the Messiah's coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/59-19.html
- Gill applies it to individual believers under Satan's attacks, with the Spirit raising up Christ as a standard. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-19.htm
- Chuck Smith's sermon notes take the KJV wording as a personal promise. The standard the Spirit raises is the Word of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Isa/Isa_57.cfm
- A Bible Hub study article connects the Spirit/wind to Pentecost and to believers resisting satanic "floods." https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_enemy_comes_in_like_a_flood.htm
- Pulpit on the first half: the nations, east and west, will be converted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 20: the main interpretive divide**
- The Redeemer is the goel, the kinsman-redeemer. Guzik: the goel only acted for those who asked for his help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-59/
- Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:26 with changes: "from Zion" and "remove godlessness from Jacob," which follows the Septuagint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-20.htm
- Readings differ on who is in view:
  - **Future conversion of the Jews.** Gill says it is not Cyrus but the Messiah, and refers not to Christ's first coming but to a later-day coming at the conversion of the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-20.htm GotQuestions likewise reads "all Israel will be saved" as Israel accepting its Messiah in the end times. https://www.gotquestions.org/all-Israel-saved.html
  - **The gospel age and the church.** Barnes: There can be no doubt that Isaiah refers here to the times of the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/romans/11-26.html Matthew Henry treats Zion as a type of the gospel church. He limits the promise to those who actually repent, not everyone in the visible church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_059.cfm Keil & Delitzsch: Zion means God's faithful church plus those who come back from apostasy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-20.htm
  - Pulpit: the prophet blends events from different periods into a single vision. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/59.htm

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: the wording echoes Genesis 17:4 and contains the seed of the new covenant in Jeremiah 31. The Spirit writes God's law in the heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/59-21.htm
- Who is "you"? Barnes says it is the faithful Hebrew people, not the prophet as Jerome thought. Clarke takes it as addressed to the Messiah, and notes that Kimchi applied it to the prophet. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/isaiah/59-21.html
- Calvin: the Spirit is joined to the word because preaching achieves nothing without the Spirit. God chooses to speak through human ministers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/59-21.html
- Matthew Henry: claims to be led by the Spirit must be tested by Scripture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/59-21.html
- GotQuestions (an end-times reading): the new covenant is fulfilled when Jesus returns to set up his kingdom. https://www.gotquestions.org/put-words-in-your-mouth.html
- Constable: the Spirit and the Word stay on God's people so they can be his witnesses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/59-21.html

**Translation note:** the NET Bible renders "Redeemer" in v. 20 as "protector." I didn't find NET's explanatory notes. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/59-20.htm
